llm_response.content:
EMPIRICAL RESEARCH PLAN  

============================================================

1. IDENTIFICATION STRATEGY  
Method: Difference-in-Differences–style panel regression with high-dimensional fixed effects (“panel FE”).  
Rationale:  

•  Daily weather is plausibly random conditional on geography and year; year-to-year fluctuations in the number of very hot (or cold) days within a county are therefore quasi-experimental shocks.  

•  The panel (1968–2002) allows us to difference out all time-invariant county factors (geology, baseline climate, socio-economic composition) with county fixed effects and to absorb nationwide shocks (medical technology, macro-economy, energy prices) with year fixed effects or, more flexibly, region-by-year fixed effects.  

•  Because treatment intensity is continuous (# of days in temperature bins), a traditional binary DID is inappropriate; the panel FE regression is the continuous-treatment analogue and satisfies the same identifying assumptions (parallel trends across dosage levels).  

•  The same design can be implemented on state-year energy data by replacing county FE with state FE.  

•  After estimating semi-elasticities, the historical coefficients can be combined with GCM-projected future temperature distributions to simulate end-of-century impacts (“plug-in” projection exercise).

2. TREATMENT AND CONTROL  

Treatment variable(s):  

T_hot_{c,t} = number of days in county c, year t with mean temperature > 90 °F  

T_cold_{c,t} = number of days < 32 °F  

(A more flexible specification uses a full set of 10°F–wide bins; one bin, 50-60 °F, is omitted as the reference.)  

Control group / counterfactual:  
The same county in years with fewer extreme-temperature days (within-county over-time comparison). Counties experiencing milder weather in a given year form the implicit control.  

Treatment timing:  
Continuous year-to-year variation; no single “event” date.  

(If one wished to look at short-run mortality spikes, a daily panel could be used, but given annual aggregation the treatment window is the calendar year.)  

3. KEY IDENTIFYING ASSUMPTIONS  

A1. Conditional exogeneity of weather shocks (within-county).  
Weather realizations are as-good-as-random after conditioning on county FE and large-area-by-year FE.  
Plausibility: High—daily weather is driven by atmospheric dynamics, not local socio-economic conditions.  

A2. Parallel trend / common growth in absence of treatment.  
Counties experiencing different numbers of extreme days would have followed similar mortality/energy trends in the absence of those extremes.  
Plausibility: Reasonable after including state-specific linear trends or region-year FE; testable via placebo weather variables (e.g., future weather).  

A3. No contemporaneous shocks perfectly collinear with extreme weather but independently affecting outcomes.  
Example threat: heat waves coincide with air-pollution spikes that themselves raise mortality.  
Plausibility: Moderate; can include precipitation, humidity, and PM2.5 controls where available.  

A4. Stable population composition within a year (SUTVA).  
Migration responses to annual weather shocks are small relative to the population and not correlated with mortality/energy outcomes within the same year.  
Plausibility: Likely satisfied for one-year windows; longer panels can include county-year age-structure controls.  

4. THREATS TO IDENTIFICATION & MITIGATION  

T1. Adaptation and technology trends (e.g., diffusion of air conditioning) could change the temperature–mortality relationship over time.  
Fix: Interact temperature bins with decade dummies; include county-specific linear (or even quadratic) trends; estimate separate coefficients for pre- and post-1990 subsamples.  

T2. Measurement error in county-level temperature due to sparse weather-station coverage (attenuation bias).  
Fix: Use inverse-distance weighting from all stations within 200 km; drop counties with < x stations or run robustness restricting to counties whose centroid is < 50 km from a station; instrument noisy county temperature with state-average temperature as a robustness check.  

T3. Omitted pollution shocks correlated with temperature.  
Fix: Control for annual county-level average ozone or PM, where available (EPA AQS started 1980); run robustness on colder-season temperatures where photochemical smog is weak; include precipitation/humidity to capture stagnation events.  

5. R CODE OUTLINE  

```r
#-----------------------------------------
# 0.  Packages
#-----------------------------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)      # fast high-dimensional FE
library(ggplot2)

#-----------------------------------------
# 1.  Data Loading
#   (assumes four csvs in /data)
#-----------------------------------------
mort   <- fread("data/mortality_county_age_year.csv")   # deaths & pop
energy <- fread("data/energy_state_year.csv")           # BTU, exp, price
weather<- fread("data/weather_county_year.csv")         # days in temp bins
ac_pen <- fread("data/ac_penetration_state_year.csv")   # optional control

#-----------------------------------------
# 2.  Variable Construction
#-----------------------------------------
# Mortality rate per 100k by county-age-year
mort[, mort_rate := deaths / population * 1e5]

# Merge weather
setkey(mort, county_fips, year)
setkey(weather, county_fips, year)
dt <- weather[mort]

# Create hot / cold variables (if not already in file)
# dt[, hot90 := days_mean_temp_gt90]
# dt[, cold32 := days_mean_temp_lt32]

#-----------------------------------------
# 3.  Main Regression: Mortality
#-----------------------------------------
# County and year FE, plus region*year FE to absorb macro shocks
dt[, region := substr(county_fips, 1, 1)]  # toy example: 9 Census regions

spec_mort <- feols(mort_rate ~ hot90 + cold32 | county_fips + region^year, 
                   data = dt, weights = ~population)

summary(spec_mort, cluster = ~county_fips)

#-----------------------------------------
# 4.  Energy Regression
#-----------------------------------------
# Collapse to state-year and merge
weather_state <- weather[, .(
  hot90 = weighted.mean(days_mean_temp_gt90, w = population), 
  cold32= weighted.mean(days_mean_temp_lt32,  w = population)), 
  by = .(state_fips, year)]

setkey(energy, state_fips, year)
setkey(weather_state, state_fips, year)
es <- weather_state[energy]

spec_energy <- feols(log(BTU_residential) ~ hot90 + cold32 | state_fips + region^year,
                     data = es, weights = ~population)

summary(spec_energy, cluster = ~state_fips)

#-----------------------------------------
# 5.  Robustness Check: Placebo (lead weather)
#-----------------------------------------
dt[, hot90_lead := shift(hot90, type = "lead"), by = county_fips]

placebo <- feols(mort_rate ~ hot90 + hot90_lead + cold32 
                 | county_fips + region^year,
                 data = dt, weights = ~population)

etable(spec_mort, placebo)

#-----------------------------------------
# 6.  Projection Exercise (pseudo-code)
#-----------------------------------------
# future_weather <- fread("data/forecast_cm3_a1fi_2070_2099.csv")
# Plug in coefficients and aggregate national-level deaths / energy
```

6. EXPECTED RESULTS  

•  Mortality: Each additional day above 90 °F raises all-age annual mortality by roughly 0.05–0.10 deaths per 100,000 (≈0.01–0.02 %). Effects concentrated among 65+ and <1 age groups. Cold days (<32 °F) raise mortality too but commonly by a smaller amount in recent decades due to better heating.  

•  Energy: A day above 90 °F increases residential BTU consumption by about 0.3 %, while an extra cold day (<32 °F) increases it by ~0.15 %.  

These priors are grounded in earlier temperature–mortality and degree-day–energy literatures.

7. VALIDITY CHECKLIST SELF-ASSESSMENT (DID / Panel FE)  

C1. Parallel trends (pre-treatment trends corroborated) …………………… 0.8  
C2. No spillovers between units (county weather unlikely to affect nearby county mortality net of own weather) …………………………… 1  
C3. Proper treatment timing (weather is realized within the year, no anticipation) …………… 1  
C4. Stable composition (migration/endogenous sorting minimal over 12-month window) ……… 0.6  
C5. Correct functional form & no differential measurement error ……… 0.7  

Average ≈ 0.82 → method judged reasonably valid given data and institutional context.
